title: IPA, The Key Works of Les Binet and Peter Field (Effectiveness Research)
text:
## The IPA Databank and the evidence base

The Institute of Practitioners in Advertising (IPA) holds the world's most rigorous body of marketing effectiveness evidence: the IPA Effectiveness Databank, built from case studies entered into the IPA Effectiveness Awards. Les Binet and Peter Field mined this Databank across a series of reports to derive evidence based rules for how advertising and marketing actually drive business results. A creative director should treat these findings as the closest thing the industry has to physics: creativity that ignores them tends to win awards and lose money.

## The Long and the Short of It (2013)

Described by the IPA as the most influential IPA Effectiveness Databank report, this work established a consistent, evidence based message about which marketing strategies to prioritise to achieve both immediate and sustained business outcomes. Its central distinction is between two jobs advertising does. Sales activation is short term: it drives response now (leads, sales, conversions) but its effect decays quickly. Brand building is long term: it works slowly, builds memory and emotional associations, and compounds over years. Short term activation cannot on its own sustain a business, because its effects fade; long term brand building is what produces durable growth.

## The 60:40 rule

The headline planning heuristic is the 60:40 split: on average, the optimum balance is roughly 60 percent of budget on long term brand building and 40 percent on short term sales activation. This is an average that varies by brand size, price, category and context, not an iron rule, but it corrects the persistent industry bias toward measurable short term response.

## Emotion beats rational persuasion over time

A core finding: emotional campaigns (those that work primarily through feeling rather than through rational message and information) produce larger and longer lasting business effects than rational campaigns. Over the long term, emotionally led campaigns are far more likely to deliver large profit gains. Fame building campaigns, ones that get a brand talked about and famous, are among the most effective of all. This is why the creative brief should aim for feeling and fame, not just a list of rational product claims.

## Later works

Marketing in the Era of Accountability (2007) was the original analysis, covering effective objective setting, the importance of fame building advertising, and the pitfalls of over prioritising short term ROI. Media in Focus (2017) updated the guidance for the digital era, on budget splits, channel selection and targeting. Effectiveness in Context (2018) showed how the optimal marketing mix differs by brand type and situation. Across the trajectory, later work has warned of a crisis in creative effectiveness (creatively awarded work losing its historic effectiveness advantage as budgets shift short term) and introduced Share of Search as a predictive measure of consumer demand. The recurring lesson for creative leaders: scale, reach, emotion and brand fame drive growth, and an obsession with short term efficiency metrics quietly starves it.

title: System1 Group, Fame, Feeling and Fluency: The Only Brand Metrics You Will Ever Need
text:
## Three mental shortcuts that drive brand choice

System1 argues that brands are chosen through three behavioural heuristics, and that a marketer's real job is to build these three shortcuts so their brand becomes the automatic, default choice requiring minimal deliberation. The three are Fame, Feeling and Fluency.

## Fame (the availability heuristic)

Fame is captured by the rule: if a brand comes readily to mind, it's a good choice. This is mental availability, how easily a brand is recalled at the moment of decision. Advertising builds Fame by getting the brand noticed, talked about and remembered, so it springs to mind in the buying situation.

## Feeling (the affect heuristic)

Feeling is captured by the rule: if a brand feels good, it's a good choice. It measures the emotional response and positive sentiment a brand evokes. Critically, System1 finds that Feeling is the strongest predictor of future market share growth. The concept of surplus Feeling, when positive emotion exceeds what a brand's current size would warrant, signals upcoming share gains; deficit Feeling signals decline. System1 measures emotional response through its Star Rating, a 1 to 5 scale derived from the intensity and balance of viewers' emotional reactions to an ad.

## Fluency (the processing fluency heuristic)

Fluency is captured by the rule: if a brand is recognisable, it's a good choice. It reflects how easily consumers recognise and process a brand through its distinctive assets: logos, colours, characters, sounds, taglines. High Fluency means the brand is instantly identified with minimal cognitive effort, which the brain reads as trustworthy and safe.

## Predictive power and a worked example

Combined, the three factors explain market share across categories and regions with an average correlation of about +0.9, making them highly explanatory of current performance, while Feeling in particular predicts future growth. The Tesco case illustrates the mechanism: its Feeling declined (happiness falling from 59 percent to 32 percent over four years), which predicted its fall from a 5-Star to a 4-Star brand, real market share loss, and its first profit warning in twenty years. For a creative director the lesson is direct: work should be judged on whether it builds Fame, generates genuine Feeling, and reinforces Fluency through consistent distinctive assets, not on whether it is merely clever or novel.

title: System1 Group, Orlando Wood on the Three Keys That Unlock Attention (Character, Incident, Place)
text:
## The three keys that unlock attention

Drawing on Orlando Wood's work (author of Lemon: How the Advertising Brain Turned Sour and Look Out), System1 argues that effective video advertising foregrounds three core narrative elements that together earn and hold attention: Character (who is involved), Incident (what happens), and Place (where it is set). These are the same devices that great storytelling has used across the whole history of advertising. Ads built from living characters, an unfolding incident, and a real sense of place engage the audience and are remembered; ads that strip them out do not.

## Right-brain versus left-brain advertising

Wood's thesis, built on the neuroscience of Iain McGilchrist, distinguishes two modes of attention. Left-brain (direct, full-frontal) advertising shows the product upfront, addresses the viewer directly, is flat, literal and abstract, relies on relevance and precise targeting, and drives immediate direct effects such as web traffic. It assumes the viewer is already interested. Right-brain (narrative, emotional) advertising features living characters, unexpected moments and believable real-world settings; it appeals to broad, vigilant, sustained attention; it generates emotional response and, per the IPA Databank, drives the major market share and profit gains.

## Why modern advertising went flat

Since around 2006 advertising has become flatter, more abstract, more rhythmic and repetitive, more self-conscious and didactic, and more reliant on words, on-screen text and voiceover. Wood attributes this to the rise of targeted digital platforms: the promise of reaching the right person at the right time reduced the perceived need for broad narrative appeal, pushing work toward product-centric, abstract presentation that lacks character depth and spatial coherence. The correction for a creative director is to put character, incident and place back into the work, because those right-brain features are what elicit emotion, hold attention, and build the brand over time.

title: Ed Catmull (Harvard Business Review), How Pixar Fosters Collective Creativity
text:
## People over ideas

Ed Catmull, cofounder and president of Pixar and Disney Animation, opens by rejecting a common belief. A studio head once told him his central problem was not finding good people but finding good ideas. Catmull disagrees: that belief is rooted in a misguided view of creativity that exaggerates the importance of the initial idea. In filmmaking and complex product development, creativity involves a large number of people from different disciplines working effectively together. The initial idea, what the movie business calls the high concept, is merely one step in a long, arduous process that takes four to five years. A movie contains literally tens of thousands of ideas. His hard-won lesson: if you give a good idea to a mediocre team, they will screw it up; if you give a mediocre idea to a great team, they will either fix it or throw it away and come up with something that works. Getting talented people to work effectively with one another takes trust and respect, which managers cannot mandate; they must be earned over time.

## Power to the creatives (filmmaker led)

Creative power in a film must reside with the film's creative leadership, not with corporate executives or a development department. Pixar's philosophy: you get great creative people, bet big on them, give them enormous leeway and support, and provide an environment in which they can get honest feedback from everyone. Pixar calls this being filmmaker led. Each person on a film should be given creative ownership of even the smallest task. Good directors harness the analytical power and life experiences of their staff; they are superb listeners who strive to understand the thinking behind every suggestion and use the best ideas regardless of where they originate.

## The Braintrust

The pillar of Pixar's peer culture is the brain trust: John Lasseter and a group of directors (the article names Andrew Stanton, Brad Bird, Pete Docter, Bob Peterson, Brenda Chapman, Lee Unkrich, Gary Rydstrom and Brad Lewis). When a director and producer feel they need help, they convene the group and show the current version of the work in progress, followed by a lively two-hour give-and-take discussion, all about making the movie better. There is no ego; nobody pulls punches to be polite; it works because all participants trust and respect one another. Crucially, after a session it is up to the director to decide what to do with the advice: there are no mandatory notes, and the brain trust has no authority. This dynamic is essential. It liberates the trust members to give unvarnished expert opinions, and liberates the director to seek help and fully consider the advice. When Pixar tried to export the model to a technical area and gave the review group authority, it stopped working; the moment they said this is purely peers giving feedback to each other, effectiveness improved.

## Dailies, candor, and safety to show unfinished work

Pixar shows daily animation work in an incomplete state to the whole crew (the dailies). Once people get over the embarrassment of showing work still in progress, they become more creative; the practice communicates points to the whole crew at once, lets people learn from and inspire each other, and removes surprises at the end. Two principles are constantly reinforced: everyone must have the freedom to communicate with anyone (the decision-making hierarchy and the communication structure are two different things), and it must be safe for everyone to offer ideas. Barriers between disciplines (class structures, different languages, physical distance) are impediments that must be torn down. John Lasseter's saying captures the technology-and-craft interplay: technology inspires art, and art challenges the technology.

## Postmortems

Pixar structures project postmortems to stimulate discussion rather than lay blame. It asks participants to list the top five things they would do again and the top five they would not; the positive-negative balance makes it a safer environment to examine every aspect of the project. Participants also bring performance data, such as how often something had to be reworked, to challenge assumptions based on subjective impressions.

title: Bill Bernbach, 1947 Letter to Grey Advertising (reproduced)
text:
## The letter that launched the creative revolution

On 15 May 1947, while still at Grey Advertising, Bill Bernbach wrote an internal letter warning his agency about where it was heading. Two years later he cofounded Doyle Dane Bernbach (DDB), whose work (most famously the Volkswagen campaign) launched what became known as the creative revolution: the idea that the creative product, not media weight or formula, is what makes advertising work. This letter is the founding statement of that philosophy and a permanent warning to any creative leader.

## The trap of bigness

Bernbach wrote that the agency was getting big, which was something to be happy about but also something to worry about. He said he was worried they would fall into the trap of bigness, that they would worship techniques instead of substance, that they would follow history instead of making it, and that they would be drowned by superficialities instead of buoyed up by solid fundamentals.

## Technicians versus the idea

His central argument distinguishes the technicians of advertising from the makers of persuasive work. There are, he wrote, many great technicians in advertising, and unfortunately they talk the best game because they know all the rules: they can tell you that showing people in an ad will get greater readership, that a sentence should be a certain length, and can give you fact after fact after fact. They are the scientists of advertising. But there is one little rub: advertising is fundamentally persuasion, and persuasion happens to be not a science but an art.

## The creed

Bernbach's vision, stated in the letter, was to prove to the world that good taste, good art and good writing can be good selling. For a creative director this is the non-negotiable standard: craft and taste are not decoration opposed to results; done right, they are the mechanism of results. The letter warns against the enduring failure mode of trusting formula and rules over a genuine idea.

title: James Webb Young, A Technique for Producing Ideas (1939), extract via The Marginalian
text:
## An idea is a new combination of old elements

James Webb Young, a legendary J. Walter Thompson advertising man, distilled the ideation process in his 1939 classic A Technique for Producing Ideas. His two governing principles: first, an idea is nothing more nor less than a new combination of old elements; second, the capacity to bring old elements into new combinations depends largely on the ability to see relationships. Creativity, in this view, is not mystical inspiration but a definite, learnable process. As Young put it, the production of ideas is just as definite a process as the production of Fords.

## The five-step method

Step 1, Gather raw material: accumulate both specific material (immersion in the product and the audience) and general material (a broad, lifelong curiosity across many fields), because new combinations draw on a well-stocked mind.

Step 2, Work the material over in the mind: mentally digest and manipulate the facts, examining each from different angles, feeling for relationships and tentative, partial combinations. This stage feels frustrating and produces no finished idea, only fragments.

Step 3, The incubation stage: drop the problem completely and turn to whatever stimulates your imagination and emotions. Hand the material over to the unconscious mind and stop straining at it.

Step 4, The birth of the idea: out of nowhere the idea will appear, typically when you are relaxed and not looking for it, after the first two stages of hard work have been genuinely done.

Step 5, Shape and develop the idea: take the fragile new idea out into the world of reality, submit it to criticism, and patiently adapt and shape it to practical usefulness. Good ideas, Young noted, have self-expanding qualities once shared with understanding people.

## Why it matters for a creative director

Young's technique reframes the brief-and-concept stage: gathering enough raw material (the deep immersion) is the real work, and the leader's job includes protecting the incubation stage rather than demanding ideas on command. It also explains why a wide, curious team beats a narrow one: more old elements means more possible new combinations.

title: James Hurman with Peter Field (Cannes Lions and WARC), The Effectiveness Code
text:
## The study

The Effectiveness Code is a 2020 whitepaper by marketing effectiveness experts James Hurman and Peter Field on behalf of Cannes Lions and WARC. They analysed and compared 4,863 effectiveness award entrants and winners from 2011 through 2019, from every major market: 1,031 cases from the Cannes Creative Effectiveness Lions database, 3,616 cases from the WARC database, and 216 cases from the IPA Databank. The goal was to give the industry a universal definition and shared language of effectiveness so it can learn from its best work.

## The Creative Effectiveness Ladder (six rungs)

The Ladder identifies the six main types of effect that creative marketing produces, set in a hierarchy from least to most commercially impactful. From level 01 (lowest) to level 06 (highest): 01 Influential Idea (over-achieve on campaign metrics); 02 Behaviour Breakthrough (change consumer behaviour); 03 Sales Spike (create short-term, temporary sales growth); 04 Brand Builder (improve brand health); 05 Commercial Triumph (create sustained sales success); 06 Enduring Icon (create long-term brand and sales growth). The lower rungs are short-term effects, the upper rungs are sustained brand-building and commercial results.

## Creative Commitment

Their central discovery: marketing effectiveness is heavily influenced by a campaign's degree of Creative Commitment, a composite measure of the media budget, the duration, and the number of media channels applied to a creative campaign or initiative. Creative Commitment correlates very tightly with effectiveness: as Creative Commitment increases, so does effectiveness. Marketers have three levers, spend, duration and number of media channels, and pulling any of them gives work an effectiveness advantage. Media spend is one dimension but not the controlling factor: even at low budgets, campaigns with longer durations and more media channels are more effective. Creativity is a fourth and highly impactful lever, because creatively awarded campaigns are much more effective overall and at every level of Creative Commitment. Alarmingly, the report documents the collapse of Creative Commitment: the average fell from 8.17 in 2014 to 5.15 in 2019, which is significantly mitigating the industry's return on investment.

## How to climb the ladder

Seven principles: set the right objectives (for a Sales Spike set a three-month objective and run a fast campaign; for a Commercial Triumph set a twelve-month objective and match the campaign duration; for an Enduring Icon plan a three-year campaign and stick with it); budget realistically (share of voice needs to be higher than share of market, so a 20 percent share brand spending only 10 percent of category spend cannot expect growth); resist the pressure to carve the budget into tiny increments; plan robust, insightful strategy; choose highly creative work, because the data is conclusive that creative-award-winning qualities are far more likely to be effective; maximise creative output using the levers of budget, duration and channels; and land and expand, meaning if a campaign is working, give it more budget, more time and more channels (if you've got a tiger by the tail, don't let go).

## The precedent: Leo Burnett's 7plus scale

The authors cite Leo Burnett's earlier solution to the same problem for creativity itself. Chief Creative Officer Michael Conrad developed 7plus, a 10-point scale that eliminated vague judgement: 10 Most Inspiring in the World, 9 New Standard in Communication, 8 New Standard in Category, 7 Excellence in Craft, 6 Fresh Idea(s), 5 Innovative Strategy, 4 Cliche, 3 Non-competitive, 2 Destructive, 1 Appalling. The target was 8 to 10, the zone to avoid was 1 to 4. Within the first five years of 7plus, 27 Leo Burnett agencies were named Agency of the Year in their countries. A shared language let the network learn from its best and lift its average.

## The anti-pattern of award cynicism

The report confronts a common cynicism: that effectiveness awards go to campaigns that were popular but didn't do much for sales, that winning is all in how well the paper is written, and that winners are the result of charm or cronyism more than rigour and real results. The Ladder exists precisely to replace that vague argument with a rigorous, shared standard.

title: IPA, The Creative Effectiveness Ladder (Cannes Lions and WARC)
text:
## A shared language for creative effectiveness

The IPA presents the Creative Effectiveness Ladder, developed by James Hurman and Peter Field for Cannes Lions and WARC from an analysis of nearly 5,000 case studies drawn from the Cannes Creative Effectiveness Lions, WARC and IPA Effectiveness Databanks (2011 to 2019). It responds to a near-unanimous view among industry leaders that the field lacks a universal definition and a shared language of effectiveness, which limits its ability to agree what best practice looks like or to learn from its best work. The Ladder is designed as a continuous improvement tool and the judging framework for future Creative Effectiveness Lions.

## Creative Commitment and the short-termism warning

Central to the framework is Creative Commitment, measured by three variables: budget investment, campaign duration, and the number of media channels deployed. The more brands increase these variables, the more likely they are to achieve creatively effective work, though benefits can plateau or fall back beyond optimal levels. The critical warning for creative leaders: the industry has shifted toward short-term campaigns using fewer channels, which correlates with decreased creative effectiveness. This mirrors the IPA's own finding of a drift away from long-running brand-building campaigns toward activation-oriented marketing, and it is precisely why creative directors should argue for scale, duration and sustained ideas rather than a stream of disposable short bursts.

title: Ogilvy, Quotations of David Ogilvy (Ogilvy 75th Anniversary Edition)
text:
## The Big Idea

From the official Ogilvy collection of David Ogilvy's quotations, curated from Confessions of an Advertising Man, Ogilvy on Advertising, How to Create Advertising That Sells, Principles of Management and early Creative Council reports. On ideas: Unless your advertising is built on a big idea it will pass like a ship in the night. Big ideas are usually simple ideas. And on where ideas come from and who has them: Senior men have no monopoly on great ideas, nor do creative people; some of the best ideas come from account executives, researchers, and others, so encourage this because you need all the ideas you can get. On the culture that produces them: encourage innovation, change is our lifeblood, stagnation our death knell.

## Brand image and positioning

Every advertisement must contribute to the complex symbol which is the brand image. The most important decision is how to position your product. But positioning without craft is empty: a lot of today's campaigns are based on optimum positioning but are totally ineffective because they are dull, or badly constructed, or ineptly written, and if nobody reads your advertisement or looks at your commercial, it doesn't do you much good to have the right positioning. Ogilvy warns against a brand trying to be all things to all people: most manufacturers are reluctant to accept any limitation on the image of their brand, they want it to be a male brand and a female brand, an upper-class brand and a plebeian brand, and they generally end up with a brand which has no personality of any kind, a wishy-washy neuter (no capon ever rules the roost). Consistency is the discipline: it takes uncommon guts to stick to one style in the face of all the pressures to come up with something new every six months; golden rewards await the advertiser who has the brains to create a coherent image and the stability to stick with it over a long period. The personality of a product is an amalgam of many things: its name, its packaging, its price, the style of its advertising, and above all the nature of the product itself.

## Respect the audience

We sell, or else. Yet you cannot bore people into buying your product; you can only interest them in buying it. And the audience deserves respect: the consumer isn't a moron, she is your wife, and you insult her intelligence if you assume that a mere slogan and a few vapid adjectives will persuade her to buy anything, because she wants all the information you can give her.

## Anti-pattern: design by committee

Ogilvy is scathing about committee work. A lot of advertisements and television commercials look like minutes of a committee meeting, and that is what they are; advertising seems to sell most when it is written by a solitary individual who studies the product, the research and the precedents, then shuts the door of his office and writes. Nowadays it is the fashion to pretend that no single individual is ever responsible for a successful advertising campaign, but this emphasis on teamwork is bunkum, a conspiracy of the mediocre majority.

## Anti-pattern: chasing awards and admiring your own cleverness

Resist the temptation to write the kind of copy which wins awards: Ogilvy says he is always gratified when he wins an award, but most of the campaigns which produce results never win awards because they don't draw attention to themselves. The idea, not the executional cleverness, is the message; it is the professional duty of the advertising agent to conceal his artifice. He cites Aeschines and Demosthenes: when Aeschines spoke, they said how well he speaks, but when Demosthenes spoke, they said let us march against Philip. Ogilvy is for Demosthenes.

title: Emma Coats, Pixar's 22 Rules of Storytelling (reproduced by Aerogramme Writers' Studio)
text:
## Pixar's 22 Rules of Storytelling

In 2011 Pixar story artist Emma Coats shared a set of storytelling guidelines that have become a canonical checklist for narrative craft, useful to any creative director building emotional, story-led work. Faithful summary of the 22:

1. You admire a character for trying more than for their successes. 2. You gotta keep in mind what's interesting to you as an audience, not what's fun to do as a writer; they can be very different. 3. Trying for theme is important, but you won't see what the story is actually about until you're at the end of it; now rewrite. 4. The story spine: Once upon a time there was ___. Every day, ___. One day ___. Because of that, ___. Because of that, ___. Until finally ___. 5. Simplify. Focus. Combine characters. Hop over detours. You'll feel like you're losing valuable stuff but it sets you free. 6. What is your character good at, comfortable with? Throw the polar opposite at them. Challenge them. How do they deal? 7. Come up with your ending before you figure out your middle. Endings are hard; get yours working up front. 8. Finish your story, let go even if it's not perfect. In an ideal world you have both, but move on. Do better next time. 9. When you're stuck, make a list of what wouldn't happen next; often the material to get you unstuck will show up. 10. Pull apart the stories you like. What you like in them is a part of you; you've got to recognize it before you can use it. 11. Putting it on paper lets you start fixing it. If it stays in your head, a perfect idea, you'll never share it with anyone. 12. Discount the first thing that comes to mind, and the second, third, fourth, fifth; get the obvious out of the way. 13. Give your characters opinions. Passive/malleable might seem likable to you as you write, but it's poison to the audience. 14. Why must you tell this story? What's the belief burning within you that your story feeds off of? That's the heart of it. 15. If you were your character, in this situation, how would you feel? Honesty lends credibility to unbelievable situations. 16. What are the stakes? Give us reason to root for the character. What happens if they don't succeed? Stack the odds against. 17. No work is ever wasted. If it's not working, let go and move on; it'll come back around to be useful later. 18. You have to know yourself: the difference between doing your best and fussing. Story is testing, not refining. 19. Coincidences to get characters into trouble are great; coincidences to get them out of trouble are cheating. 20. Exercise: take the building blocks of a movie you dislike. How would you rearrange them into what you do like? 21. You gotta identify with your situation and characters; you can't just write cool. What would make you act that way? 22. What's the essence of your story? The most economical telling of it? If you know that, you can build out from there.

## Why it matters for a creative director

The story spine (rule 4) is a portable structure for building emotional narrative in a campaign, and rules 14, 16 and 19 name the discipline that separates a real story from decoration: a reason it must be told, real stakes, and earned (not convenient) turns. This is the craft behind the emotional, right-brain advertising the effectiveness evidence rewards.

title: Nielsen Norman Group, Design Thinking 101
text:
## What design thinking is

Nielsen Norman Group defines design thinking as an ideology and an accompanying process which assert that a hands-on, user-centric approach to problem solving can lead to innovation, and that innovation leads to differentiation and competitive advantage. For a creative director, this is the discipline that keeps communication grounded in a real human problem rather than starting from an execution.

## The three-phase framework and six-step model

The process is organised into three phases: Understand, Explore and Materialize. Within these sit six steps. Empathize: conduct research to understand what users do, say, think and feel. Define: combine the research into a point of view and identify where users' problems and opportunities for innovation exist. Ideate: generate a wide range of creative ideas addressing unmet user needs. Prototype: build tactile, tangible representations to test which components work. Test: return to users for feedback on whether the solutions meet their needs. Implement: put the vision into effect, which NN/g calls the most important part of design thinking, and the one most often forgotten.

## Divergent and convergent, iterative not linear

The framework alternates divergent thinking (generating many possibilities) with convergent thinking (narrowing to a decision), moving between the problem space (understanding the real need) and the solution space (building the answer). How Might We questions turn insights into open, solvable problem statements. The process is iterative and cyclical rather than strictly linear: teams routinely loop back to earlier phases, because building a real prototype reveals what further research is needed. Applied to a creative brief or campaign, design thinking forces the team to earn the idea from a defined human need and to test it, not to fall in love with the first execution.

title: Paul Feldwick, The Anatomy of Humbug (summary via Alex Murrell)
text:
## Many theories of how advertising works, none the whole truth

Paul Feldwick, a former BBH and DDB planning head, argues in The Anatomy of Humbug that there is no single correct theory of how advertising works. He lays out several competing models. Each has its uses and its limitations, they are not mutually exclusive, and several can operate in one piece of communication. The crucial and repeated warning: any theory is dangerous if taken too literally as the whole truth. This is the intellectual humility a creative leader needs when a client or colleague insists there is one right way.

## The models

Advertising as salesmanship: the traditional view that ads work through rational, verbal arguments to an attentive audience who comprehends, believes, remembers and is persuaded (the reason-why, USP tradition of Claude Hopkins and Rosser Reeves). Advertising as seduction: much of advertising's effect is unconscious, working through non-verbal association, emotion, imagery, symbols and metaphor that charm below conscious awareness. Advertising as salience: advertising is mere publicity that simply makes a brand more mentally available through distinctive communication that generates fame, supported by a high share of voice (the Ehrenberg tradition). Advertising as social connection: how something is said (tone, manner, belonging) matters as much as what is said, and brands work as badges of shared identity. Advertising as showmanship: in the P.T. Barnum tradition, advertising arrests and attracts public attention and creates public conversation by entertaining the masses, not worrying too much about how it does it.

## The anti-pattern Feldwick attacks

His central critique is the entrenched dominance of the salesmanship model: the assumption that advertising must always be a rational sales message with a unique selling proposition, comprehended and believed. That assumption blinds the industry to the emotional, symbolic, famous and entertaining ways real advertising actually works. For a creative director, Feldwick is a licence to build work that seduces, entertains and becomes famous, and a caution against reducing every brief to a rational claim.

title: Design Observer, Helmut Krone, Period (on the DDB art director)
text:
## The page as a package

Helmut Krone was the art director whose work on Volkswagen and Avis at Doyle Dane Bernbach defined the visual language of the creative revolution. His governing belief was that the whole page is the unit of design, not the individual elements. In his words, the page ought to be a package for the product: it should look like the product, smell like the product, and every company and every product needs its own package. Art direction, in this view, is the construction of an unmistakable, ownable look, not decoration applied after the copy is written.

## The art director and copywriter as one team

Krone's method depended on the DDB innovation of putting the copywriter and art director in the same room as equal partners. On the legendary Volkswagen Think Small ad, copywriter Julian Koenig proposed the line and Krone at first protested, I suppose you want me to make the car small, before arriving at the tiny car in the upper corner that Koenig called the peculiar genius of Helmut. Layout and copy were made together, each shaping the other.

## Restraint, distinctiveness, and fighting logos

Krone described his method as Umgekehrt, turned around slightly: revolution through thousands of precise, incremental shifts within a conventional structure rather than wholesale novelty. He made deliberate, consistent typographic choices (Futura Bold for Volkswagen, a modified face for Avis) and held them for decades to build a durable brand signature. His most quoted conviction is an attack on decorative branding: I've spent my whole life fighting logos; logos say I am an ad, turn the page. For a creative director the lesson is that distinctiveness and consistency of craft, held over years, is what makes work ownable and effective, and that obvious ad-signals repel the audience.

title: Helmut Krone, Interview (on layout, craft and what counts as new)
text:
## Layout as a lost art

In this interview the DDB art director Helmut Krone treats layout as a discipline most people have abandoned. He says almost no one is looking around for a brand new page, a new way of putting down the same old elements, a new way of breaking up that 7 by 10 area. The craft is not decoration but finding a genuinely new structure for the same components.

## Layout drives copy, not the reverse

Krone pioneered letting the visual layout dictate the writing. He recounts that he actually cut the widows into the first Volkswagen ads with a razor blade and asked Julian Koenig to write that way, deliberately breaking the text so it would not sit as a solid block. This produced the clipped copy style Bill Bernbach later called subject, verb, object: a writing rhythm that emerged from a design decision.

## The imaginary line, not petty perfection

Krone's standard was effect, not finish. He describes having an imaginary line, and you have to get over that line; as soon as he feels he is over that line, he quits. If the page has the effect he was after, he is not interested in petty little corrections. This is a discipline of knowing when the idea is working and stopping, rather than polishing indefinitely.

## What new really means, and a swipe at awards

Krone defines the standard bluntly: new is when you've never seen before what you just put on a piece of paper. He is dismissive of awards culture, observing that medal-winning work typically represented innovations that were already a year or two old. For a creative director this sets a hard, original standard for craft and a warning that award fashion lags real invention.

title: Rory Sutherland (Ogilvy), on Behavioural Economics and Psychological Value (Thought Economics interview)
text:
## Advertising creates psychological value

Rory Sutherland, Vice Chairman of Ogilvy and founder of its Behavioural Science Practice, argues that effective marketing changes perception rather than the product itself, and that this perceived, psychological value is real value. Brands and advertising add worth by reframing meaning: Diamond Shreddies were merely square cereal rotated 45 degrees to look diamond-shaped, yet the reframe created a sensation, and Netflix's early appeal was psychological (no late fees, no anxiety) more than technological. For a creative director, the idea itself is the value-creation mechanism, not a wrapper around a fixed product.

## Decisions are not a logic problem

Sutherland's core caution: people don't think what they feel, don't say what they think, and don't do what they say, so standardised market research often loses the really valuable information, which lives in the outliers and anomalies rather than the averages. Human decisions run on emotional and irrational frameworks that data misses. A creative leader should treat pure rational optimisation with suspicion.

## Context, signalling, and the danger of over-optimisation

The opposite of a good idea can be another good idea, because context determines what works; this flexibility guards against being enslaved to a single methodology. Advertising spend itself functions as costly signalling: the visible expense communicates commitment and confidence in the product, which is part of why heavy brand investment works even when direct ROI looks unclear. And an obsession with data-driven optimisation eliminates experimentation and makes competitors indistinguishable, pushing everyone into brutally competitive red-ocean sameness. Discovery, he argues, requires permission for apparent irrationality, which is exactly the license a creative director must defend.

title: Creative Salon, Fifty Years of Planning and Why Stephen King Still Matters
text:
## The Planning Cycle

Stephen King of J. Walter Thompson (with Stanley Pollitt of BMP) founded the discipline of account planning in London in 1968, and his most enduring contribution is the Planning Cycle: a deceptively simple framework of five commonsense questions (where are we, why are we there, where could we be, how could we get there, are we getting there) that needs no proprietary methodology, jargon or acronyms. It gives a creative brief a rigorous, evidence-based spine and corrects briefing by gut feeling.

## Discipline in service of creativity, not against it

The crucial point for a creative director is that King saw planning as a genuine partnership with creative people, not a constraint on them. He insisted that planning must actively stimulate imagination and creativity, and that rigorous analysis should liberate creative thinking rather than suppress it. His discipline was demanding on the fundamentals: absolute clarity about who you are speaking to and what desired response you want, because human behaviour remains relatively constant even as the industry churns.

## The brand as a coherent whole and the scientific stance

King approached brands as integrated entities requiring consistent strategic thinking across every touchpoint, moving beyond narrow product-focused marketing. His intellectual legacy was to give planning credibility by pairing academic rigour with an honest acknowledgement of creativity's messy, circular nature: he treated strategy like scientific discovery, developing a hypothesis and genuinely testing to disprove it rather than merely confirming what he already believed. The single-minded discipline of the brief, one clear proposition and one desired response, is the direct descendant of this thinking.

title: Massimo Vignelli, The Vignelli Canon
text:
## Semantics, Syntactics, Pragmatics

Massimo Vignelli, one of the great modernist designers, organises design thinking in The Vignelli Canon around three aspects. Semantics is the search for the meaning of whatever we have to design; it is the first step in any assignment, understanding the problem's essence before any visual solution. Syntactics is the discipline of design itself: the grid, typeface selection, typographic hierarchy, structure and compositional order, the rigour that holds a piece together. Pragmatics is usefulness and clarity: that the solution is genuinely useful and understandable to its intended audience. A creative director can read these three as the sequence meaning, structure, usefulness that any communication must satisfy.

## The Intangibles

Beyond structure, Vignelli names the qualities that elevate work: Discipline (foundational, because design without it becomes anarchy), Appropriateness to context and purpose, Visual Strength, Intellectual Elegance over mere decoration, Timelessness that resists ephemeral trends, and Responsibility to the viewer and to culture. These are standards of taste and craft, not options.

## Against fashion and visual junk

Vignelli expresses deep skepticism toward fashion-driven design and what he calls the vulgarity of visual junk. He argues for work that transcends momentary trends through principled, purposeful thinking, treating design as a serious discipline requiring both intellectual rigour and ethical commitment. For a creative leader the transferable conviction is that discipline, appropriateness and timelessness beat novelty for its own sake, and that chasing the trend of the moment is a failure of craft.

title: Bill Bernbach, Core Principles (via Branding Strategy Insider)
text:
## Truth, insight and the human heart

Bill Bernbach, cofounder of Doyle Dane Bernbach and the father of the creative revolution, built his philosophy on truth and human insight rather than formula. In his words: the most powerful element in advertising is the truth. And: it is insight into human nature that is the key to the communicator's skill. A creative director's first job, on this view, is to find the true and human thing about the product and say it in a way people feel.

## Creativity as an economic force, not decoration

Bernbach insisted that creativity pays its way. Properly practiced creativity can make one ad do the work of ten. Properly practiced creativity must result in greater sales more economically achieved. This reframes craft as leverage: the better idea does more work per dollar, so pushing for a stronger idea is a commercial act, not an indulgence.

## Difference and the impression you make

On distinctiveness: in advertising not to be different is virtually suicidal. And on what actually accumulates in the audience's mind: nobody counts the number of ads you run, they just remember the impression you make. This is an argument for fewer, braver, more memorable executions over a high volume of forgettable ones.

## Persuasion is an art, and the product still matters

Advertising is fundamentally persuasion, and persuasion happens to be not a science but an art. Yet Bernbach was honest about the limits of advertising: advertising doesn't create a product advantage, it can only convey it, and a great ad campaign will make a bad product fail faster. The idea amplifies the truth of the product; it cannot substitute for it. For a creative leader this is both a licence to be bold and a discipline to stay truthful.

title: Cannes Lions, Creative Strategy Lions (the idea behind the idea)
text:
## The idea behind the idea

Cannes Lions, the global benchmark for creative excellence, defines the Creative Strategy Lions as celebrating the idea behind the idea: how strategic planning can redefine a brand, reinvent its business, and influence consumers or wider culture. This names a distinction a creative director must hold: the executional idea (the ad) sits on top of a deeper strategic idea (the insight and the move), and the strategic idea is what the industry's highest honour actually rewards.

## The judging criteria and what excellence means

The Creative Strategy award is scored on weighted dimensions: 30 percent on exceptional interpretation of the business or brand challenge, 30 percent on breakthrough thinking, 20 percent on the creative idea itself, and 20 percent on measurable outcomes and results. Winning work must display transformational problem solving and deep cultural insight. Across the Lions, creative excellence is defined by the artistry, skill, talent and flair required to deliver beautifully executed ideas with the power to cut through and bring the creative idea to life (craft), while the Creative Effectiveness Lions celebrate the measurable impact of creative work that met its business objectives and drove sustainable impact over time. For a creative leader the lesson is that craft, strategy and effectiveness are one system: a beautiful execution with no strategic idea behind it, or no measurable result, is not excellent by this standard.

title: IPA / Peter Field, The Crisis in Creative Effectiveness (anti-pattern)
text:
## The myth that creativity cannot be measured, refuted and then a warning

Peter Field's IPA report The Crisis in Creative Effectiveness is the definitive rebuttal to the myth that creativity cannot be measured, and simultaneously a warning about how the industry has broken its own creative advantage. Analysing nearly 600 IPA case studies from 1996 to 2018, Field documents that creatively awarded campaigns, which for decades were dramatically more effective than non-awarded campaigns, have fallen to their lowest effectiveness levels in over two decades and have lost their historical advantage over non-awarded work.

## The three conclusions

The report states three findings plainly. First, short-termism drives the collapse in creative effectiveness and efficiency. Second, lessons from creative best practice can reverse the damage. Third, the industry urgently needs to change the way it identifies and rewards creativity. In Field's own words: despite our warnings, the misuse of creativity has continued to grow and the effectiveness advantage has continued to decline. It follows the IPA's 2016 report Selling Creativity Short, which warned of the dangers of short-termism and a misunderstanding of how brands grow.

## The anti-pattern for a creative director

The lesson is not that creativity stopped working, but that creativity aimed at short-term activation and applause instead of long-term brand building loses its power. Chasing awards for their own sake, and starving brand building to fund short bursts, are the failure modes that hollow out creative effectiveness. A top creative leader treats creativity as a measurable driver of sustained business results and argues, with this evidence, against the short-term reflex.

title: Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Maximise Distinctive Assets (brand codes)
text:
## Branding without the brand name

The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute (home of Byron Sharp and Jenni Romaniuk) defines distinctive assets as the elements that uniquely evoke the brand, such as logos, taglines, colours, shapes and characters. They function as branding without the brand name: learned cues that let category buyers notice, recognise and recall the brand even when the name is not shown. For a creative director these are the ownable brand codes that campaign after campaign should build and reuse, not discard.

## Three principles to build distinctive assets

Reach: assets must be presented through mass advertising to achieve fame among both customers and non-customers. Co-presentation: brand assets should consistently appear alongside the brand name so the audience learns to anchor the connection. Commitment: longevity is key, because teaching consumers takes time and repetition (the Institute cites Audi's roughly 40-year commitment to its tagline as an example of the discipline required).

## Brand-led creativity and the consistency discipline

Strong distinctive assets enable brand-led creativity and work across every environment, retail, digital, radio and video, allowing a brand to remain recognisable regardless of budget. The transferable lesson for a creative leader is that the craft is consistency: reinventing the whole look every campaign destroys the very codes that make a brand recognisable and cheap to notice. The creative job is to keep the codes alive and fresh, not to throw them away for novelty.

title: Howard Ibach, Thoughts on Writing the Creative Brief: The Single-Minded Proposition
text:
## The single-minded proposition

Howard Ibach, author of How To Write A Single-Minded Proposition, treats the single-minded proposition (SMP) as the hardest group of words to write in the entire brief, because it carries so much weight. Its purpose is to inspire the creative team to find the Big Idea. It goes by many names (One Key Thing, Unique Selling Proposition, Single Most Important Thing) but always resolves to one especially relevant, resonating, compelling idea: one point that gets through, expressed in no more than one sentence.

## Write it like the first ad, like a billboard

The SMP should function as the first ad for the project. Ibach's test is to think of a billboard rather than a paragraph, because the best billboards are short, very short: the proposition should be short, quick, headliney, tagliney. He offers a vivid exercise: imagine you have to shout your message to someone across a crowded Broadway in Times Square. You cannot yell an entire paragraph, or even a long sentence, so the discipline of the crowded street forces genuine single-mindedness.

## Technique and example

One emotional route is to complete the sentence, when I use or drive or experience the product, I feel ___, and mine the answer for the proposition. For a Volkswagen Beetle convertible campaign, Ibach offers the SMP Woe isn't you, showing how brevity plus emotional resonance beats a list of features.

## The anti-pattern of the unfocused brief

The failure mode is a proposition that is not single-minded: an unedited first draft that tries to carry several benefits at once, which reveals a lack of confidence and gives the creative team nothing sharp to leap from. A brief with two or three propositions is a brief with none. The other elements of the brief exist to support the one proposition, which is why Ibach saves the SMP for last.

title: D&AD, Creativity: Dead or Alive?
text:
## Creativity's state depends on what you do next

D&AD, the British body founded in 1962 to promote excellence in design and advertising, frames the modern anxiety about creativity as a choice rather than a fate. Its central line: whether you think creativity is dead or you think it's alive, you're right, its state depends on what you choose to do next. The threat is not technology but abandonment: technology isn't stealing creativity, we're abandoning it, we're scrolling instead of making.

## Prove it through what you make

D&AD's core standard for a creative leader is bias to action and craft: creativity must prove itself alive through what we make, not what we discuss, strategise, or endlessly refine. This is a direct warning against the anti-pattern of an industry that thinks itself to a standstill, mistaking endless strategising and refinement for the actual work of making something. D&AD also recognises that creativity has expanded beyond traditional agencies into brand teams, independent creators and grassroots makers, and treats that democratisation as a positive evolution.

## The takeaway for a creative director

Guard against paralysis by analysis. Strategy and refinement matter, but they are in service of making, and a creative culture stays alive by producing brave, well-made work rather than by talking about it. The leader's job is to keep the team making, experimenting and shipping excellent, original work.
